section.title: The Vision of the Four Beasts
section.sectionRationale: The book turns from court narratives to Daniel's own visions, and this first vision is the hinge of the whole book. Four monstrous beasts rise from the sea, a blasphemous little horn wages war on the saints, and then the Ancient of Days convenes His court and gives an everlasting kingdom to one like a son of man and to the saints of the Most High. It re-tells the four-kingdom scheme of chapter 2 from heaven's side, with judgment and the triumph of God's people at its center.
section.thesis: History's brutal empires rise like beasts from the churning sea and a defiant horn oppresses the saints for an appointed season, but the Ancient of Days holds court, strips the beasts of power, and gives an everlasting, indestructible kingdom to one like a son of man and to the saints of the Most High.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the four beasts from the sea; the Ancient of Days seated for judgment; one like the Son of Man given everlasting dominion; the interpretation, four kings but the saints receive the kingdom; and the fourth beast, the little horn, and the everlasting kingdom of the saints.

units.label: The four beasts from the sea

verses.text: In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar over Babylon, Daniel had a dream, and visions passed through his mind as he lay on his bed. He wrote down the dream, and this is the summary of his account.
Daniel declared: “In my vision in the night I looked, and suddenly the four winds of heaven were churning up the great sea.
Then four great beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others:

The first beast was like a lion, and it had the wings of an eagle. I watched until its wings were torn off and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man and given the mind of a man.

Suddenly another beast appeared, which looked like a bear. It was raised up on one of its sides, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth. So it was told, ‘Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!’
Next, as I watched, suddenly another beast appeared. It was like a leopard, and on its back it had four wings like those of a bird. The beast also had four heads, and it was given authority to rule.

After this, as I watched in my vision in the night, suddenly a fourth beast appeared, and it was terrifying, dreadful and extremely strong, with large iron teeth. It devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left. It was different from all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns.

While I was contemplating the horns, suddenly another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were uprooted before it. This horn had eyes like those of a man and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance.

units.label: The Ancient of Days seated for judgment

verses.text: As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the {{attiq_yomin|Ancient of Days}} took His seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of His head was like pure wool. His throne was flaming with fire, and its wheels were all ablaze.
A river of fire was flowing, coming out from His presence. Thousands upon thousands attended Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him. The court was convened, and the books were opened.
Then I kept watching because of the arrogant words the horn was speaking. As I continued to watch, the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire.
As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was removed, but they were granted an extension of life for a season and a time.

units.label: One like the Son of Man

verses.text: In my vision in the night I continued to watch, and I saw One like the {{bar_enash|Son of Man}} coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence.

And He was given {{shaltan|dominion}}, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.

units.label: The interpretation: the saints receive the kingdom
units.note: four kings, but the saints inherit

verses.text: I, Daniel, was grieved in my spirit, and the visions in my mind alarmed me.
I approached one of those who were standing there, and I asked him the true meaning of all this. So he told me the interpretation of these things:
‘These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.
But the {{qaddishin|saints}} of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever, yes, forever and ever.’

Then I wanted to know the true meaning of the fourth beast, which was different from all the others, extremely terrifying, devouring and crushing with iron teeth and bronze claws, then trampling underfoot whatever was left.

I also wanted to know about the ten horns on its head and the other horn that came up, before which three of them fell, the horn whose appearance was more imposing than the others, with eyes and with a mouth that spoke words of arrogance.
As I watched, this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them,
until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom.

units.label: The fourth beast and the everlasting kingdom

verses.text: This is what he said: ‘The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth, different from all the other kingdoms, and it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it.
And the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom. After them another king, different from the earlier ones, will rise and subdue three kings.

He will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints of the Most High, intending to change the appointed times and laws; and the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.
But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever.

Then the sovereignty, dominion, and greatness of the kingdoms under all of heaven will be given to the people, the saints of the Most High. His kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all rulers will serve and obey Him.’
Thus ends the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale. But I kept the matter to myself.”

attiq_yomin.gloss: The Ancient of Days, literally the one advanced in days. It is a title for God as the eternal Judge, seated on a fiery throne with countless attendants and the books of judgment open. Against the raging beasts of history, He is the calm, everlasting King who convenes the court and settles every account.

bar_enash.gloss: One like a son of man, a human figure in contrast to the beasts. He comes with the clouds of heaven, a mark of deity, and receives everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days. Jesus made this His favorite self-title, and at His trial He applied this very verse to Himself; the phrase names both His true humanity and His divine, universal reign.

shaltan.gloss: Dominion, authority, rule. The beasts are given a limited shaltan that is stripped away, but the son of man is given an everlasting shaltan that will never pass away or be destroyed. The word contrasts the passing power of empires with the unshakable reign handed to Christ and shared with His people.

qaddishin.gloss: The holy ones, the saints. The saints of the Most High are oppressed by the arrogant horn for an appointed season, but the court finds in their favor and they receive and possess the everlasting kingdom. The word gathers God's suffering people into the triumph of the son of man, who reigns and shares His kingdom with them.

basic.context: Daniel now becomes the one who dreams. He sees four terrifying beasts rise from a stormy sea, the last with ten horns and a small, boastful horn that attacks God's people. Then the scene shifts to heaven: the Ancient of Days takes His throne, a court is seated, the books are opened, and the beast is judged. One like a son of man comes on the clouds and is given an everlasting kingdom, and the saints of the Most High are told they will receive and possess that kingdom forever.
basic.hermeneutics: This vision covers the same ground as chapter 2's statue, four kingdoms replaced by God's everlasting reign, but seen from heaven, as a courtroom drama of judgment and vindication. The details of the beasts and horns are debated, and wise readers hold them humbly. The unmistakable center is clear: God judges the proud powers, the son of man reigns forever, and the persecuted saints inherit the kingdom.
basic.originalLanguages: The eternal Judge is the attiq yomin, the Ancient of Days. The human figure who receives everlasting rule is the bar enash, one like a son of man. His shaltan, dominion, never passes away, unlike the beasts. And the qaddishin, the saints of the Most High, share in that everlasting kingdom.
basic.typology: The one like a son of man, coming on the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom, is fulfilled in Jesus, who took this title as His own. The heavenly court where the books are opened foreshadows the last judgment, and the vindication of the persecuted saints anticipates the final triumph of God's people in Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus called Himself the Son of Man more than any other title, and at His trial He quoted this very scene, claiming to be the one who comes on the clouds to reign. The everlasting dominion given here is His. He is both the human representative of God's people and the divine King, and He shares His kingdom with the saints who suffered with Him.
basic.god: God is the Ancient of Days, the eternal Judge enthroned above the chaos of history. However fierce the beasts, however loud the boasting horn, God sits in unshaken majesty, convenes His court, and gives the verdict. He limits the time of evil, vindicates His people, and hands the everlasting kingdom to His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 2 tells the same four kingdoms as a statue. Matthew 26 records Jesus applying the son of man coming on the clouds to Himself. And Revelation 1 and 5 show the risen Christ with hair white as wool, receiving the kingdom and reigning forever.
basic.oneStory: History looks like a sea of monsters, one empire devouring the next, and God's people crushed under a blasphemous power. But heaven's court has the last word: the beasts are judged, the Son of Man is crowned, and the saints inherit an everlasting kingdom. This is the hope of the whole Bible, fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of Man who reigns and will share His reign with all who are His.

context.literary:
Chapter 7 is the hinge of the book, and the way it is built shows why. The Aramaic section that began at Daniel 2:4 ends here, and the Hebrew resumes in chapter 8. Inside the Aramaic section the chapters pair up in a mirror pattern. Chapter 2 and chapter 7 both give four kingdoms followed by God's everlasting kingdom. Chapters 3 and 6 are stories of faithful servants delivered from death by a decree. Chapters 4 and 5 are the two stories of kings humbled by God. Chapter 7 returns to the opening vision of the statue, but from a new angle. Chapter 2 saw the empires as a human eye would see them, a glittering image of metal. Chapter 7 sees them from heaven's side, as hungry animals.

The chapter itself is arranged in three scenes and an interpretation. Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, verses 2 to 8; the scene shifts to a throne room where the court sits, verses 9 to 12; and a human figure approaches the throne and receives the kingdom, verses 13 and 14. Daniel then asks one of the attendants, and the interpretation in verses 15 to 27 is given in two stages, a short answer in verses 17 and 18 and a long one in verses 19 to 27 about the fourth beast. The proportions are the message. The first three beasts take a verse each; the fourth takes the rest, and the interpreter spends more words on the horn than on all the earlier empires.

The throne room scenes in verses 9 to 10 and 13 to 14 move into a more elevated, poetic rhythm, with short lines about fire, wool and the river. Everything else is told in plain narrative. The contrast does its own work: the beasts come with noise and teeth, the throne comes with stillness and light.

The chapter ends with Daniel pale and troubled, who 'kept the matter to myself,' verse 28. The vision that opens the book's prophetic half closes on a man who has seen more than he can carry.
context.historical:
The date in verse 1, the first year of Belshazzar, is about 553 BC, which means the vision came some years before the feast of chapter 5. The book arranges its materials by theme, not by calendar, and moves the vision to its place after the court stories so that the visions can follow the tales. For an exile in Babylon, Babylon was still the world's great power, and the hope of a kingdom beyond it must have seemed fantastic.

The sea in verse 2 had a long history in the imagination of the ancient Near East as the home of chaos and monsters. In Israel's own poetry God subdues that chaos: He 'smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea,' Psalm 74:13, and in the last day He will 'slay the dragon of the sea,' Isaiah 27:1. For a Babylonian court the sea was where the gods fought monsters; here the monsters are empires, and the God who sits above the sea is Israel's. The four winds that churn it suggest that the powers rise by God's permitting.

The beasts resemble the animals that the prophets use for judgment. Hosea 13:7-8 pictures God as a lion, a leopard and a bear, and in Revelation 13:2 the beast from the sea combines all three. The first beast, a lion whose wings are torn away and who is made to stand like a man, is a picture of a proud power brought low, and it echoes Nebuchadnezzar's own humbling, Daniel 4:16, when he was given the mind of a beast.

If the fourth kingdom is Rome, the vision spans from Babylon to the world of the New Testament. If the fourth is Greece, the little horn is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who in 167 BC desecrated the temple, outlawed Jewish practice and persecuted faithful Jews, 1 Maccabees 1. Either way, the text is addressed to people who would feel a persecuting power in their own lives.
context.canonical:
Daniel 7 became one of the most quoted chapters in the New Testament and in later Jewish and Christian writing. The Son of Man is the most important single figure of the Gospels, and nearly every use of the title falls under the shadow of this chapter. When Jesus answers the high priest at His trial, He joins two texts: He says that they will see the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven,' Mark 14:62, and Matthew's version reads 'coming on the clouds of heaven,' Matthew 26:64. The first phrase comes from Psalm 110:1 and the second from Daniel 7:13. The high priest understands exactly what is being claimed.

Other New Testament writers pick up the same image. Stephen sees 'the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,' Acts 7:56. Revelation 1:7 announces that 'He is coming with the clouds,' and in Revelation 1:13 to 14 the risen Christ appears as 'One like the Son of Man' with hair 'white like wool, as white as snow,' which is the description of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9 given to Jesus. In Revelation 13 the beast from the sea is built from Daniel's beasts, with the same arrogant mouth, the same war on the saints and the same limit of 42 months, which is 'a time, times, and half a time,' Revelation 12:14.

The promise to the saints is taken up too. Jesus tells His little flock that the Father is 'pleased to give you the kingdom,' Luke 12:32, and Paul says that the saints will judge the world, 1 Corinthians 6:2. Revelation 20:4 pictures thrones set, with those seated on them 'given authority to judge,' and Revelation 5:10 says that Christ's people will reign. And the opened books of Daniel 7:10 return at the last judgment, Revelation 20:11-12, linked to the book that will deliver God's people in Daniel 12:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The vision is addressed to a people who, in the author's lifetime, lived under one empire after another and expected to live under worse. The author means to turn their eyes from the surface of history to its centre. The empires look like unrivalled powers, but in heaven's view they are beasts that come up out of a sea they did not make, and each is permitted to rule for a season and a time, verse 12.

He also means to prepare them for the possibility that the worst will happen. The fourth beast and the horn are not softened. The horn 'was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them,' verse 21, and the saints are 'given into his hand' for a limited time, verse 25. The author does not tell the faithful that they will escape. He tells them that persecution is real and that it is bounded, and that the court in heaven will rise on the day appointed.

And he means to give them a reason to hold on. The repeated promise is that the saints will 'receive the kingdom and possess it forever,' verse 18, and the structure of the interpretation makes it the main thing. Everything on earth, the beasts, the horns and the war, is placed inside a frame whose ending is the gift of the kingdom. The reader is asked to stay faithful, as Daniel 3 and 6 showed, because the story already has its ending.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a vision, and its purpose is to be understood and trusted, not to be turned into a timetable. The details of the beasts and horns are not commands, and the numbers, 'a time, times, and half a time,' are given in a symbolic style that has been read in several ways. The text itself shows how to read it: the interpreter gives a short answer in verses 17 and 18 and says plainly what the beasts are, 'four kings,' and who wins.

What the chapter does prescribe is by implication. The believer is asked to measure the powers of the world by what they will become before the throne and not by how they look now. It also describes a faithful response to a terrifying vision. Daniel is not calmed by being told that all will be well; he is 'grieved in my spirit' and alarmed, verse 15, and he asks for the true meaning. The people of God may be troubled by what they see, and they may seek understanding from the one who knows.

The chapter does not give licence to name a modern ruler as the little horn, or to fix the time of the end by calculation. Jesus Himself said that no one knows the day or the hour, and the history of such predictions is a warning. What carries forward is the shape: arrogant power for a limited time, a court that sits, and a kingdom given to the saints.

debates.question: Who is the one like a son of man in verse 13?

views.label: The Messiah, a divine and human King
views.case: He comes with the clouds of heaven, a divine prerogative, receives worship and an everlasting kingdom, and is presented as an individual; Jesus applied this very verse to Himself at His trial, so Christians read Him as the Messiah, both truly human and truly divine.

views.label: A representative of the saints, corporately
views.case: The interpretation says the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom, so some read the son of man as a symbol for God's people, the human figure standing over against the beastly empires; on this view the individual and corporate readings converge in the King who embodies His people.

debates.bearing: The New Testament resolves the two: the Son of Man is Jesus, the divine-human King who reigns forever and includes His people in His reign, so that His victory is theirs.

debates.question: What is the fourth beast and its little horn?

views.label: Rome and a later blasphemous power
views.case: Read alongside chapter 2's iron kingdom, the fourth beast is often identified with Rome, and the little horn with a future antichrist figure who wars on the saints for a time, times, and half a time before God's court destroys him, a pattern Revelation develops.

views.label: Greece and Antiochus IV
views.case: Reading Media and Persia as separate beasts makes the fourth beast Greece, and the little horn Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple and persecuted the Jews, changing the sacred times and laws, before his power was broken.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree on the point that matters: a defiant power will oppress God's people for a limited, appointed time, and then the heavenly court will strip away its dominion and give the everlasting kingdom to the saints.

debates.question: Who are the saints of the Most High?

views.label: The faithful people of God
views.case: The saints are persecuted, given into the horn's hand, and finally given the kingdom, verses 21, 25 and 27. That describes human believers who suffer and are vindicated, and the New Testament takes it that way, Revelation 13:7 and 20:4. Jews and Christians have read the phrase this way.

views.label: Heavenly beings, the angelic host
views.case: The Aramaic phrase uses the plural of the word for the Most High, and 'holy ones' elsewhere in Daniel can mean angels, as in 4:13. Some therefore read the saints as God's heavenly court, who receive the kingdom on behalf of His people. Verse 27 calls them 'the people, the saints of the Most High,' which keeps the earthly people in view.

debates.bearing: The immediate point is not affected. The kingdom is given to those who belong to the Most High, and they share the reign of the Son of Man, which is how the New Testament reads it.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in this chapter explain how the vision works. The first is the court. In verse 10 the court 'was convened,' and the Aramaic word is dina, the word for judgment and a seat of judgment. It returns in verse 22, where the Ancient of Days 'pronounced judgment in favor of the saints,' and in verse 26, where 'the court will convene.' The picture is one of legal process, with a verdict that is given in favour of those who had been losing. The saints do not take the kingdom by force. It is awarded to them by a court.

The verb 'given' is the quiet engine of the chapter. The beasts are repeatedly given things: the leopard 'was given authority to rule,' verse 6, the first beast 'given the mind of a man,' verse 4, and the little horn is allowed to speak. Then in verse 14 the human figure 'was given dominion, glory, and kingship,' and in verse 27 the kingdom is 'given to the people.' Nothing in the chapter is seized. Every dominion is a gift, which means every dominion can be taken back, and the same hand that lends authority to the beasts gives it to the Son of Man.

The word for 'serve' in verse 14, where all peoples 'should serve Him,' and in verse 27, where all rulers 'will serve and obey Him,' is the same verb that Daniel 6:16 and 6:20 use for Daniel's service of God. In Daniel 3 it is what the friends refuse to give to the king's gods. It is the language of worship as much as of obedience, and in this chapter the service of every nation is directed to the human figure.

The word 'arrogance' in verses 8 and 20 translates a word that means literally great things. The horn has a mouth that speaks great things, and the pairing of that with the boasting mouth is the author's sign of a ruler who speaks as only God should. When verse 25 says that he will speak 'against the Most High,' the same mouth is turned to blasphemy. The horn also intends 'to change the appointed times and laws.' The word for appointed times, from the root that also gives the word for season, is the same one that Daniel 2:21 uses when it says that God 'changes the times and seasons.' The horn is claiming the prerogative that belongs to God, and that is why the court acts.

The word for 'a time' in 'a time, times, and half a time,' verse 25, is a general word for a set period, the same one used for the 'seven times' that passed over Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 4:16. On the common reading the phrase counts out to three and a half, half of the complete seven. It reads as a limited period, shorter than full and fixed by God, and whether it is a literal span or a symbol of a cut-short time is a matter on which readers differ. In verse 12 the beasts whose dominion is removed are given 'an extension of life for a season and a time,' using the same pair, so the lives of the empires are measured out in the same units as the horn's war.

Finally, the plural in verses 18, 22, 25 and 27, where the saints are of the 'Most High,' uses the plural form of the word for high, a plural of majesty or of the heights. The form gathers the heavenly and earthly sense and is part of why the identity of the saints is discussed. Verse 13 says the human figure 'was led into His presence,' using a verb that means to be brought near, which is the language of priestly and royal approach. The Son of Man is not seizing the throne; He is presented.

typology.type: The human figure over the beasts, Daniel 7:3-14
typology.fulfillment: Humanity was made to rule over the creatures, Genesis 1:26, and Psalm 8:6 says that everything was placed under man's feet. In Daniel's vision the creatures that rule are beasts, and the human figure at last receives dominion. Hebrews 2:5-9 takes the same thread and says that we do not yet see everything subject to man, 'But we see Jesus,' crowned with glory and honor. The escalation in Christ is that He is the true human who recovers what Adam lost, and does so by suffering death. The correspondence falls short where the vision falls silent: Daniel does not say how the human figure gains the kingdom, and the New Testament says it is by the cross.

typology.type: The cloud, the approach and the throne, Daniel 7:13-14
typology.fulfillment: A figure comes with the clouds, approaches the Ancient of Days and is given everlasting dominion. The Gospels set this alongside what happened when Jesus rose. A cloud took Him from the disciples' sight, Acts 1:9, and He was seated 'far above all rule and authority, power and dominion,' Ephesians 1:20-22. Jesus says, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18, using the language of a gift. The same figure will come again, and Revelation 1:7 says 'He is coming with the clouds.' The type is a vision of enthronement; its fulfilment is both the ascension and the return, and Daniel's picture covers both without separating them.

typology.type: The little horn who speaks against the Most High, Daniel 7:8, 25
typology.fulfillment: The horn is a human ruler who exalts himself, speaks arrogantly, persecutes the saints and tries to change God's laws and times. In history this was seen in Antiochus IV, and in the New Testament Paul describes a 'man of lawlessness' who will 'seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God,' 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4. John says that there are already 'many antichrists,' 1 John 2:18, and Revelation 13:5-7 gives the beast a mouth for blasphemy and war against the saints for 42 months. The pattern repeats and grows: each such figure is a smaller copy of the final one. The type falls short in that none of the earlier horns could do what the last will attempt, and none will survive the court.

typology.type: The saints who suffer and then reign, Daniel 7:18, 27
typology.fulfillment: The saints are given into the horn's hand and then receive the kingdom. The pattern of suffering followed by glory is the life of Christ and of His people. Paul says that we are 'co-heirs with Christ,' if we suffer with Him so that we may be glorified with Him, Romans 8:17, and 'if we endure, we will also reign with Him,' 2 Timothy 2:12. Jesus promises the one who overcomes the right to sit with Him on His throne, Revelation 3:21. The saints share the reign of the Son of Man because they are united to Him, and the type holds only on that condition: the kingdom is theirs because it is first His.

study.christ:
Daniel 7 is the most important Old Testament source for the way Jesus spoke about Himself. 'Son of Man' is His favourite title, and the Gospels use it more than any other, so a reader who knows Daniel 7 hears a good deal more in the title than the words suggest. It is a human title, and also the name of the figure who comes to the throne of God and receives a universal, everlasting kingdom. At His trial Jesus brought the two together. Asked whether He is the Christ, He said that the high priest would see 'the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven,' Mark 14:62. The high priest tore his robes, because to come with the clouds is to share a prerogative that belongs to God.

The chapter leads to Christ by the figure of the one who is both human and given divine honour. The beasts are monstrous and come from below; the Son of Man is a man and comes from above. He approaches the Ancient of Days and is brought into His presence. He is distinct from the Ancient of Days, and yet all peoples serve Him, using a verb that elsewhere in Daniel is used of the worship of God. The New Testament takes that tension seriously. Jesus 'has been given' all authority, Matthew 28:18, and the Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22, 'because He is the Son of Man,' John 5:27, which is exactly the Daniel 7 combination of a human figure with the right to judge.

It leads to Him by the scene of the opened books. The final judgment in Revelation 20:11 to 12 follows Daniel 7:9 to 10, and Christ is the judge. The saints do not stand alone before the court, because the Son of Man is both their judge and their representative. His victory is theirs: the Father 'is pleased to give you the kingdom,' Luke 12:32, and in Christ His people are 'a kingdom and priests,' Revelation 5:10.

It leads to Him by the way the kingdom is won. Daniel sees the dominion given; the New Testament says how. 'Worthy are You,' the heavenly song says, 'because You were slain,' Revelation 5:9. The Lamb's death is the road to the Son of Man's throne, and Philippians 2:9 to 11 says that He was exalted to the highest place because He first humbled Himself to death on a cross.

A caution is in order. The beasts, the horns and the numbers are not all pointers to Jesus, and many details of Daniel 7 are in debate. The reading above rests on the New Testament's own use of the Son of Man and the throne room, not on finding a Christ in every wing and tooth.
study.god:
The great fact about God in this chapter is where He sits. In the middle of a vision that begins with churning water and savage beasts, the scene opens on a throne that is set in place, and the Ancient of Days takes His seat, verse 9. The terror of the first eight verses is a real terror, but it is not the whole. God does not leap into the sea to fight. He sits down. That is the posture of a judge, a king who is not threatened.

He is eternal. The title Ancient of Days stands against kingdoms that last a generation. The empires rise one after another, each different from the last, and each takes its turn on stage. The God who sits has no succession. He is the only one whose throne does not pass to another.

He is holy and fiery. His clothing is white as snow, His hair is like pure wool, and His throne is flaming with fire and its wheels ablaze, verse 9. A river of fire comes out from His presence, verse 10. The language of fire recalls the throne chariot of Ezekiel 1, where a figure like a man sits above a throne of sapphire. Holiness in Scripture is not abstract; it is the quality that cannot be touched by evil without consuming it. The horn's arrogance is no match for it.

He is just, and His justice is procedural. The court sits, the books are opened and the horn is judged in light of what is written. The beast is slain not by rage but by verdict, verse 11. This tells us that God's judgment is not arbitrary, and that it does not happen secretly. He judges in the open, with a court before Him, and in favour of those who have suffered. The judgment given 'in favor of the saints,' verse 22, is the vindication of the oppressed.

He is sovereign over the powers. The other beasts have their dominion taken away but keep a season and a time, verse 12. Every empire is allowed to exist for as long as He allows, and no longer. The persecution of the saints is limited by Him: they are given into the horn's hand for a stated time, verse 25. Nothing that happens to God's people is outside His timing.

He is generous. The kingdom that He gives to the Son of Man He then shares with the saints. The God of this chapter does not hoard His rule. He gives it to one who is human and to a people who are His own, and that gift has no end.

For worship, the chapter gives us a posture. Daniel is shaken to the core and his face pales, verse 28, and the proper response to such majesty is not to explain it away but to be stilled by it. At the same time, because the throne is occupied and the verdict is already coming, we can face the beasts of our own day with steadiness.

crossReferences.note: In the statue vision the God of heaven sets up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor left to another people. Daniel 7 tells the same story from heaven's side, and the repeated promise shows that the author of the book means the two visions to interpret each other.

Jesus tells the high priest that he will see the Son of Man at God's right hand and coming with the clouds of heaven. By joining Psalm 110 with Daniel 7:13, He claims the throne of God and the dominion given to the human figure, which is why the council calls it blasphemy.

John sees One like the Son of Man whose hair is white like wool, as white as snow. The imagery that Daniel gave to the Ancient of Days, Daniel 7:9, is given to the risen Christ, so the two figures of Daniel's vision are brought together in the one who is at once human and divine.

A beast rises from the sea with ten horns, like a leopard with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. John merges Daniel's first three beasts into one and gives it the dragon's authority, so that the sea beast is the final form of the powers that Daniel saw.

The writer quotes Psalm 8 about man's rule over creation, admits that we do not yet see everything under his feet, and says 'we see Jesus.' This is the New Testament's answer to the dominion given to a human figure in Daniel 7, though the writer does not name that chapter.

At the end of the book Michael will stand, a time of distress will come, and everyone whose name is found written in the book will be delivered. The books opened in Daniel 7:10 and the book that saves in 12:1 belong to the same court.

Ezekiel sees a throne of sapphire and, above it, a figure like a man. His throne chariot with its wheels of fire stands behind Daniel's wheels ablaze in 7:9, so the vision of a human figure enthroned in glory was already part of Israel's prophetic language.

The psalmist recalls that God 'smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea.' The sea monsters of Daniel 7:2 to 3 live in this tradition of chaos that God has defeated, and the vision declares that He will again subdue the powers that rise from it.

Paul writes of a man of lawlessness who opposes and exalts himself above every object of worship, and sits in the temple of God proclaiming himself to be God. The description echoes the horn who speaks against the Most High and seeks to change God's times and laws.

John sees a great white throne, the dead standing before it, and books opened. The final judgment fulfils Daniel 7:9 to 10, and the presence of the Book of Life gives the vision its saving edge: judgment is also the place where God's people are vindicated.

Jesus tells His little flock not to be afraid, because their Father is pleased to give them the kingdom. The saints of Daniel 7:18 receive the kingdom as a gift, and the Father's pleasure in giving it is what the little flock is asked to rest in.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 gave humanity the task of ruling over the creatures of the earth and sea, and Genesis 3 saw that task slip away to a serpent. Daniel 7 is the Bible's own picture of what that loss has become: beasts rise from the sea and rule, each hungrier than the last, and the human beings they rule are trampled. Seen in this light, the chapter is not an odd piece of apocalyptic imagery but the Genesis story continued. The question it raises is whether the dominion that was lost will ever be recovered.

The answer is the human figure at the throne. A man is brought into the presence of the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory and kingship, and all the peoples serve Him. What Adam was made for and failed to do is given to another, and then shared. The vision joins Eden's promise to the end of the book, where the saints reign.

It also gathers what comes before. The exiles' question was whether the God of Israel had lost to Babylon and whether the empires would last. Chapter 2 answered with a statue struck by a stone; chapter 7 answers with a court and a verdict. Both say that the empires have an appointed end and a kingdom follows.

And it sets up all that comes after. The visions of chapters 8 to 12 will fill in the details of the powers, the persecution and the deliverance. The Gospels take the Son of Man and make Him the Man of Nazareth, who goes to the cross and rises. The letters of the New Testament tell the church that it lives between the first coming and the last, in the time of the horn, while the Son of Man reigns. And Revelation draws the beasts, the court and the throne into its picture of the last days, with the dragon, the sea beast and the Lamb.

The story ends where Daniel 7:27 says it will: sovereignty, dominion and greatness 'under all of heaven' given to the people of the Most High, and all rulers serving and obeying Him. In the new creation, Revelation 22:5 says, the servants of God will reign forever and ever. The sea from which the beasts came is gone, Revelation 21:1, and there is no more chaos from which monsters can rise. The throne at the centre is the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the one who sits on it has no rival.

quiz.q: What do the four beasts rising from the sea represent?

options.text: Four kings or kingdoms that arise from the earth, a succession of worldly empires.
options.note: Daniel 7:17 interprets the beasts as four kings who arise.

options.text: Four literal animals sent to punish Babylon.
options.note: They are symbols of kingdoms, not literal animals.

options.text: Four false gods of the nations.
options.note: They picture political kingdoms, not gods.

options.text: The four seasons of the year.
options.note: The beasts stand for successive empires, not seasons.

quiz.q: Who is the Ancient of Days in the vision?

options.text: God, the eternal Judge, enthroned in fire, who convenes the court and opens the books.
options.note: Daniel 7:9-10 pictures God as the everlasting Judge over history.

options.text: The oldest of the four kings.
options.note: He is not a king of the beasts but God Himself, seated in judgment over them.

options.text: An angel who guards the throne.
options.note: He is God the Judge, not merely an attending angel.

options.text: The little horn grown old.
options.note: The horn is judged by the Ancient of Days, who is God.

quiz.q: What is given to the one like a son of man?

options.text: Everlasting dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will never be destroyed, served by all peoples.
options.note: Daniel 7:14 describes his eternal, universal reign.

options.text: A temporary rule that will later pass to another.
options.note: The opposite; his dominion will not pass away and his kingdom cannot be destroyed.

options.text: Command over the four beasts as their leader.
options.note: He receives an everlasting kingdom from God, not leadership of the beasts.

options.text: Only the land of Judah.
options.note: His dominion is over every nation and language, not one land.

quiz.q: What happens to the saints of the Most High in the end?

options.text: After being oppressed for an appointed time, they are vindicated and receive the everlasting kingdom.
options.note: Daniel 7:18, 22, 27 promise the saints will possess the kingdom forever.

options.text: They are destroyed along with the beasts.
options.note: The opposite; they inherit the kingdom after their suffering.

options.text: They are left out of the kingdom entirely.
options.note: They receive and possess the kingdom forever.

options.text: They become the fifth beast.
options.note: They are God's holy people, given the kingdom, not another beast.

quiz.q: How does the Son of Man vision point to Jesus?

options.text: Jesus took the title Son of Man and applied this coming with the clouds to Himself, claiming the everlasting kingdom.
options.note: Jesus quotes Daniel 7:13 at His trial, Matthew 26:64.

options.text: It describes a purely symbolic figure with no link to any person.
options.note: The New Testament identifies the Son of Man as the real, personal Christ.

options.text: It predicts a Roman emperor who would help the Jews.
options.note: The everlasting, worshiped King is Christ, not a Roman emperor.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: Jesus explicitly claimed this vision as speaking of Himself.

questions: Daniel saw history as a sea of beasts, yet God enthroned above it all. When the news feels like one monster after another, how does the throne of the Ancient of Days steady you?
The boastful horn was given only a set time, times, and half a time. How does knowing that evil has an appointed limit shape the way you endure hard seasons?
The Son of Man reigns forever and shares His kingdom with the saints. What difference does it make to know that suffering with Christ leads to reigning with Him?
Heaven's court opened the books and gave the verdict. How does the certainty of God's final judgment comfort you, and how does it sober you?
Daniel was deeply troubled by what he saw, yet he trusted God. How do you hold on to faith when God's ways in history are frightening or hard to understand?

translationNotes.note: The great sea may refer to the Mediterranean, but as apocalyptic imagery the churning sea pictures the restless chaos of the nations from which empires arise.
One like the Son of Man may be rendered one like a son of man; the New Testament repeatedly applies this coming with the clouds to Jesus, as the cross references show.
A time, and times, and half a time is a symbolic span, often taken as three and a half units, denoting a limited period of persecution set by God, echoed in Revelation.
The verse marks the close of the Aramaic section of Daniel, which began at 2:4b; from chapter 8 the book returns to Hebrew.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Daniel 7:1-28. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose. Chapter 7 completes the Aramaic section, so load-bearing lexicon entries use Aramaic.
